title: Comparison of the Efficacy of Different First‐Line Therapies for EGFR L858R‐Mutated NSCLC Patients With Brain Metastases
author: Jing Chen; Yin Pan; Baishen Zhang; Meichen Li; Hui Yu; Mingjie Yu; Likun Chen
text:
ABSTRACT
Compared to exon 19 deletions, the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) exon 21 L858R (21L858R) mutation is associated with a poorer prognosis in non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), particularly in patients with brain metastases (BMs). However, there is a notable lack of prospective or retrospective clinical studies focusing on this specific population. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy of different first‐line treatment strategies using EGFR‐tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) in NSCLC patients harboring the 21L858R mutation and BMs while providing insights into concurrent mutations and resistance mechanisms. We analyzed clinical data from 331 patients diagnosed with the EGFR 21L858R mutation and BMs who received first‐line EGFR‐TKI treatment at Sun Yat‐sen University Cancer Center between April 2014 and June 2023 (ID: GASTO‐1027). The efficacy was evaluated through intracranial progression‐free survival (iPFS), PFS, and overall survival (OS). Compared to the first‐generation and second‐generation cohorts, the third‐generation EGFR‐TKI cohort demonstrated significant improvements in iPFS (p = 0.002), PFS (p < 0.001), and OS (p = 0.016). Within the third‐generation EGFR‐TKI group, the combination chemotherapy cohort exhibited the most favorable outcomes, with marked extensions in both iPFS (p = 0.037) and PFS (p = 0.049). Multivariate analyses identified the treatment regimen of third‐generation TKIs combined with chemotherapy as an independent prognostic factor for improved iPFS. Compared to treatment regimens containing first‐generation or second‐generation EGFR‐TKIs, patients with TP53 mutations derived greater benefit from treatment regimens containing third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs. The combination of third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs with chemotherapy shows enhanced efficacy in patients with EGFR 21L858R mutations and BMs compared to other treatments. Future prospective clinical trials are essential to assess this combination's effects in this population.
Keywords: brain metastases, chemotherapy, L858R, non‐small cell lung cancer, tyrosine kinase inhibitors
The combination of third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs with chemotherapy shows enhanced efficacy in patients with EGFR 21L858R mutation and BMs compared to other treatments. Future prospective clinical trials are warranted to assess this combination in this population. Compared to treatment regimens containing first‐generation or second‐generation EGFR‐TKIs, patients with baseline concurrent mutations, particularly TP53 mutations, derived greater benefit from treatment regimens containing third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs. Patients treated with third‐generation TKIs in combination with antiangiogenic therapy exhibited a significantly higher incidence of MET amplification resistance mutations compared to those receiving monotherapy.

1. Introduction
Non‐small cell cancer (NSCLC) remains one of the leading causes of cancer‐related mortality worldwide [1]. Targeted therapy for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) sensitizing mutations represents a significant breakthrough in the treatment of NSCLC in the new century [2]. The exon 19 deletion (19del) and exon 21 L858R (21L858R) mutations are the two most common types of EGFR mutations and are the primary determinants of clinical response to EGFR‐tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) [3, 4, 5]. However, in most trials involving EGFR‐TKIs, the efficacy of these agents in patients with the 21L858R mutation was lower than that in patients with the 19del mutation [6, 7]. For instance, patients with the 19del mutation treated with first‐line osimertinib demonstrated a progression‐free survival (PFS) of 21.4 months, whereas those with the 21L858R mutation had a PFS of only 14.4 months [8]. Furthermore, patients with the 21L858R mutation did not show improved overall survival (OS) compared to those treated with first‐generation TKIs [9]. Therefore, overcoming resistance associated with the 21L858R mutation remains a critical area of research.
Approximately 40%–50% of patients with NSCLC develop brain metastases (BMs) during their disease, with those harboring EGFR mutations facing an even higher risk [10, 11, 12, 13]. The treatment of NSCLC patients with BMs is particularly challenging and associated with a poor prognosis. In the context of EGFR‐TKI therapy, patients with BMs and 21L858R mutation derive significantly less benefit compared to those with 19del. In a Phase II clinical trial evaluating gefitinib for Japanese patients with BMs from EGFR‐mutant lung adenocarcinoma, 21L858R mutation was associated with poorer outcomes after treatment with gefitinib in both PFS (p = 0.003) and OS (p = 0.025) compared to 19del mutation [14]. Similarly, a pooled analysis of LUX‐Lung 3 and LUX‐Lung 6 studies focusing on patients with BMs reported that in those with 19del mutation, afatinib significantly improved PFS compared to chemotherapy (9.5 vs. 4.7 months, hazard ratio [HR] = 0.24, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.09–0.62). In contrast, among patients with 21L858R mutation, there was no significant difference between afatinib and chemotherapy (6.9 vs. 9.7 months, HR = 0.90, 95% CI: 0.36–2.27) [15]. Therefore, improving treatment outcomes for NSCLC patients with BMs harboring 21L858R mutation is of paramount importance.
Recent studies have indicated that combining EGFR‐TKIs with chemotherapy or antiangiogenic therapy may improve clinical outcomes for patients with EGFR‐mutant NSCLC and BMs [16, 17]. However, the efficacy of these treatment regimens in patients with BMs harboring 21L858R mutation remains unclear, and the optimal first‐line treatment strategy has yet to be definitively established.
Currently, there are no prospective or retrospective clinical studies specifically addressing patients with BMs harboring EGFR 21L858R mutation. Therefore, this study retrospectively analyzes the efficacy of various EGFR‐TKI treatment patterns as first‐line therapy in patients with EGFR L858R‐mutated NSCLC and BMs. The aim is to identify the optimal systemic treatment strategy for these patients while also exploring the impact of concurrent mutations on treatment efficacy and the mechanisms of resistance associated with first‐line therapy.
2. Methods
2.1. Patients
We retrospectively identified NSCLC patients with EGFR 21L858R mutation and BMs who received first‐line EGFR‐TKI treatment from April 2014 to June 2023 at Sun Yat‐sen University Cancer Center. The data cutoff date for follow‐up was August 2024. The main inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) histologically or cytologically confirmed NSCLC; (2) BMs identified by magnetic resonance imaging at the time of diagnosis; (3) EGFR 21L858R mutation verified by Amplification Refractory Mutation System PCR or next generation sequencing (NGS); (4) first‐line treatment after diagnosis was EGFR‐TKI or EGFR‐TKI combination therapy; (5) available clinical data and follow‐up information.
2.2. Treatment Regimens
In a retrospective analysis of clinical data from 331 patients with EGFR 21L858R mutation NSCLC and BMs, we categorized the patients into three cohorts based on the generation of EGFR‐TKIs administered: the first (1st) cohort comprised 186 patients treated with first‐generation TKIs; the second (2nd) cohort included 16 patients who received second‐generation TKIs; and the third (3rd) cohort consisted of 129 patients treated with third‐generation TKIs. The third cohort was further divided into three groups based on the treatment regimen: Group A included 79 patients receiving third‐generation TKIs as monotherapy; Group B comprised 30 patients receiving third‐generation TKIs in combination with chemotherapy; and Group C consisted of 20 patients receiving third‐generation TKIs combined with antiangiogenic therapy.
First‐generation EGFR‐TKIs included gefitinib, erlotinib, and icotinib; second‐generation TKIs consisted of afatinib and dacomitinib; and third‐generation TKIs included osimertinib, aumolertinib, and furmonertinib. In the combination treatment, the chemotherapy regimen consisted of pemetrexed combined with a platinum‐based agent, while the antiangiogenic therapy included bevacizumab, anlotinib, and apatinib. The specific distribution of patients within each treatment group is detailed in Table S1.
2.3. Data Collection and Clinical Efficacy Evaluation
Clinical information was collected, including but not limited to demographic information, smoking history, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) score, histological types, metastases sites, current or subsequent mutations, and details of first‐line treatment regimens.
First, we conducted an efficacy comparison analysis of different first‐line treatment regimens. Clinical response to first‐line treatment was retrospectively evaluated by the investigators based on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) scan reports and clinical documentation during treatment, in accordance with RECIST 1.1. The intracranial PFS (iPFS) was defined as the period from first‐line treatment to intracranial disease progression or death. PFS was defined as the period from the start of first‐line treatment to disease progression or death. Intracranial objective response rate (ORR) was defined as the percentage of patients achieving a complete response or partial response of intracranial lesions. OS was defined as the period from the onset of first‐line treatment to death. Additionally, we analyzed the relationship between concurrent mutations and the efficacy of different treatment regimens. Finally, we summarized the mechanisms of resistance associated with the various treatment patterns.
The primary end point was iPFS. The secondary end points included PFS and OS.
To explore treatment resistance mechanisms, NGS was performed on tissue or plasma samples collected at the time of disease progression following first‐line treatment. Biopsy sites were determined based on clinical judgment and included both intracranial and extracranial progressing lesions. In most cases, samples were obtained from progressing extracranial sites (e.g., lung, lymph nodes, pleura, and liver), while a minority involved cerebrospinal fluid specimens. Resistance mechanisms were defined as newly acquired mutations, amplifications, or pathway alterations detected at the time of progression, which were not present at baseline.
2.4. Statistical Analysis
Descriptive statistics were used to summarize all variables. Categorical variables were analyzed using appropriate statistical tests such as chi‐square or Fisher's exact test. Survival data were estimated using Kaplan–Meier curves and compared using a log‐rank test. The risk of disease progression and death was evaluated using the Cox proportional hazards regression model, and HR and 95% CI were calculated. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analyses were conducted to assess the prognostic value for iPFS. Variables with a p value < 0.1 in the univariate analysis were selected for the multivariate Cox regression model. In addition, brain localized therapy was included in the model due to its potential clinical relevance, regardless of statistical significance. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 25 and R software, version 4.4.1. A two‐sided p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
3. Results
3.1. Baseline Patient Characteristics
In total, 331 NSCLC patients with EGFR 21L858R mutation and BMs were eligible for inclusion in our study (Figure S1). Regarding first‐line EGFR‐TKI treatment, 186 patients (56.2%) received either first‐generation EGFR‐TKIs as monotherapy or in combination; 16 patients (4.8%) received second‐generation EGFR‐TKIs as monotherapy or in combination; and 129 patients (39.0%) received third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs as monotherapy or in combination. Table 1 shows the baseline characteristics of patients. Overall, the median age was 58 years (range: 28–83). The majority were female (61.6%), had extracranial metastases (70.7%), and had no neurological symptoms (82.8%). Only 90 patients (27.2%) received brain localized therapy. Among these 90 patients, 56 received stereotactic radiosurgery, 12 received whole brain cranial irradiation, and 22 received brain surgery. There was no difference in clinicopathological characteristics between the three treatment groups.

3.2. Treatment Patterns and Efficacy Analysis
3.2.1. Efficacy Analysis of First‐, Second‐, and Third‐Generation TKI
In all patients, the median iPFS of the 3rd cohort was significantly longer (20.6 months, 95% CI: 16.8–24.4, p = 0.002, Figure 1A) than that of the 1st (15.1 months, 95% CI: 13.4–16.8) and 2nd cohorts (13.5 months, 95% CI: 7.4–19.5). Similarly, the 3rd cohort showed significantly longer PFS (18.6 months, 95% CI: 15.5–21.7, p < 0.001, Figure 1B) than that of the 1st (12.8 months, 95% CI: 11.0–14.5) and 2nd cohorts (10.4 months, 95% CI: 3.1–17.7). More importantly, the 3rd cohort was markedly associated with longer OS (41.2 months, 95% CI: 36.6–45.7, p = 0.016, Figure 1C) than that of the 1st (30.7 months, 95% CI: 28.0–33.0) and 2nd cohorts (26.9 months, 95% CI: 9.7–44.0). Pairwise comparison of efficacy analysis between the 3 cohorts can be found in Table S2.
In terms of treatment response, the iORR of the 3rd cohort (77.3%, 95% CI: 68.0–84.5) was significantly higher than that of the 1st (62.3%, 95% CI: 54.0–70.0) and 2nd cohorts (61.5%, 95% CI: 35.5–82.3) (p = 0.046, Table S3).
These results indicated that third‐generation TKIs may offer favorable efficacy compared to first‐ and second‐generation TKIs; however, the observed differences should be interpreted with caution due to potential selection bias arising from the imbalanced sample sizes across the treatment cohorts, particularly the small number of patients in the second‐generation group. We subsequently conducted a further efficacy analysis of third‐generation TKI treatment patterns to identify the optimal therapeutic strategy for NSCLC patients with EGFR 21L858R mutation and BMs.
3.2.2. Efficacy Analysis of Different Treatment Patterns of the Third‐Generation TKI
A total of 129 patients received first‐line third‐generation EGFR‐TKI treatment, of which 79 patients (61.2%) were treated with third‐generation TKIs as monotherapy (Group A), 30 patients (23.3%) received third‐generation TKIs in combination with chemotherapy (Group B), and 20 patients (15.5%) were treated with third‐generation TKIs in combination with antiangiogenic therapy (Group C). Table 1 presents the baseline characteristics of patients in Groups A, B, and C.
The median iPFS was 16.6 (95% CI: 11.8–21.4) months in Group A and 21.0 (95% CI: 14.7–27.3) months in Group C, while not reached with only 7 cases of disease progression in Group B (p = 0.037, Figure 2A). In comparison to Group A (16.1 months, 95% CI: 12.9–19.3) and C (17.8 months, 95% CI: 9.1–26.6), the median PFS in Group B was significantly longer (28.0 months, 95% CI: 19.4–not reached, p = 0.049, Figure 2B). Likewise, the median OS was 40.3 (95% CI: 28.6–52.0) months in Group A and 53.3 (95% CI: 31.8–not reached) months in Group C, while not reached with only 4 deaths in Group B (p = 0.090, Figure 2C). Pairwise comparison of efficacy analysis between 3 groups can be found in Table S2.
In terms of treatment response, the iORR in the combination therapy Groups B (89.3%, 95% CI: 72.8–96.3) and C (89.5%, 95% CI: 68.6–97.1) was higher than that of the monotherapy Group A (66%, 95% CI: 52.2–77.6) (p = 0.023). Group B exhibited the highest ORR at 81.5% (95% CI: 63.3–91.8) (p = 0.023) (Table S4).
Both univariate (HR = 0.37, 95% CI: 0.17–0.82, p = 0.014) and multivariate Cox survival analyses (HR = 0.37, 95% CI: 0.17–0.82, p = 0.013) demonstrated that the combination therapy of third‐generation TKIs with chemotherapy was an independent prognostic factor for iPFS (Table 2).

3.2.3. Comparative Efficacy of Third‐Generation EGFR‐TKIs Plus Chemotherapy Versus First‐Generation EGFR‐TKIs‐Based Combination Therapies
To further evaluate whether the combination of third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs with chemotherapy offers superior clinical benefit compared to first‐generation EGFR‐TKI‐based combination regimens, we performed a subgroup analysis of patients treated with third‐generation TKIs plus chemotherapy (3rd + chemo, n = 30), first‐generation TKIs plus chemotherapy (1st + chemo, n = 32), and first‐generation TKIs plus antiangiogenic therapy (1st + antiangio, n = 42).
Patients receiving 3rd + chemo exhibited the most favorable outcomes compared to the 1st + chemo and 1st + anti‐angio groups (p = 0.001, Figure S2A). Similarly, the median PFS was significantly longer in the 3rd + chemo group than in the 1st + chemo and 1st + anti‐angio groups (p < 0.001, Figure S2B). As for OS, the 3rd + chemo group had not reached median OS at data cutoff, while the 1st + chemo and 1st + anti‐angio groups showed median OS of 26.0 months (95% CI: 21.1–31.0) and 27.4 months (95% CI: 18.7–36.0), respectively (p = 0.002, Figure S2C).
3.3. Efficacy Analysis of Concurrent Mutations and Various Treatment Patterns
A total of 151 patients had baseline NGS data, among which 59 patients (39.1%) in the 1st cohort, 8 patients (5.3%) in the 2nd cohort, and 84 patients (55.6%) in the 3rd cohort. We next compared the relationship between concurrent mutations and efficacy in patients receiving first‐ or second‐generation TKIs versus those receiving third‐generation TKIs. The baseline characteristics of the concurrent mutations are presented in Figure 3. The majority of patients (80.8%, 122/151) exhibited concurrent mutations. The three most common concurrent genes identified were TP53, EGFR (amplifications or other mutations), and RBM10.
We analyzed the iPFS, PFS, and OS of patients treated with first‐ or second‐generation TKIs versus third‐generation TKIs based on the presence or absence of concurrent mutations, including TP53 mutations and EGFR mutations (amplifications or other mutations). Patients with concurrent mutations derived significantly greater benefits in OS from third‐generation TKI treatment (Figure 4A, Figure S3A–C). Particularly, patients with TP53 mutations demonstrated more pronounced improvements in iPFS, PFS, and OS when treated with third‐generation TKIs (Figure 4B,C, Figure S3A–C).
3.4. Distinct Resistance Mechanisms to Different Treatment Patterns
We analyzed the mechanisms of resistance in NSCLC patients with EGFR 21L858R mutation and BMs after different first‐line treatments. Among 126 patients undergoing NGS after treatment, 59 received first‐generation TKIs alone, 37 received first‐generation TKIs with chemotherapy or antiangiogenic therapy, 7 received second‐generation TKIs alone, 17 received third‐generation TKIs alone, and 6 received third‐generation TKIs combined with antiangiogenic therapy. The seven main mechanisms of resistance were the emergence of T790M mutations, TP53 mutations, mutations in cell cycle pathway genes, MET amplification, EGFR amplification, other EGFR mutations, and mutations in MAPK/PI3K pathway genes. A detailed comparison of the resistance mechanisms associated with each treatment regimen is presented in Figure 5. T790M mutation remained the dominant mechanism of resistance for first‐ and second‐generation TKIs. Combination therapy with first‐generation TKIs showed a lower incidence of T790M‐resistant mutations than monotherapy (p = 0.088), although this did not reach statistical significance. Third‐generation TKIs combined with antiangiogenic therapy led to a significantly higher incidence of MET amplification than monotherapy (p = 0.01).
3.5. Adverse Events
Adverse events (AEs) were recorded in all treatment groups. Among the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation EGFR‐TKI cohorts, the overall incidence of any‐grade AEs was similar (Table S5).
We further analyzed AEs among patients receiving different 3rd‐generation EGFR‐TKI regimens (Table S6). The most frequently observed AEs included rash, diarrhea, and neutropenia. Grade ≥ 3 AEs were more commonly observed in patients receiving combination regimens. Specifically, neutropenia (23.3%) was the most frequent grade ≥ 3 AE in patients receiving third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs plus chemotherapy. Treatment interruption due to AEs occurred in 3 patients (3.8%) in Group A, 4 patients (13.3%) in Group B, and 3 patients (15.0%) in Group C. Most AEs were manageable with supportive care and did not result in permanent treatment interruption.
4. Discussion
This study provides a comprehensive evaluation of first‐line treatment strategies in NSCLC patients with EGFR 21L858R mutation and BMs, a population with distinct clinical behavior and therapeutic challenges. In addition to assessing the efficacy of different generations of EGFR‐TKIs, we examined the impact of concurrent genomic alterations and resistance mechanisms on treatment outcomes. The results indicate that regimens containing third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs achieve more favorable intracranial and systemic control than those based on first‐ or second‐generation TKIs. Moreover, the combination of third‐generation TKIs with chemotherapy was associated with the most prolonged iPFS and PFS, highlighting its potential as a preferred therapeutic approach in this setting.
Treating NSCLC patients with EGFR 21L858R mutation and BMs is challenging. These patients benefit less from EGFR‐TKI therapy compared to those with 19del mutation. A meta‐analysis showed that the benefit of EGFR‐TKIs was 50% greater for tumors with 19del mutation (p < 0.001) [18]. In patients with BMs, the efficacy of EGFR‐TKIs also appears to be less for those with 21L858R mutation [19, 20]. Zhao et al. [21] found that osimertinib provided the best PFS for patients with 19del mutations, while gefitinib plus chemotherapy was most effective for those with 21L858R mutations. This indicates that the optimal treatments may vary by mutation subtypes. With advancing therapies, treatment benefits for NSCLC patients with 21L858R mutation or BMs are improving, though conclusions remain uncertain. The FURLONG study found that furmonertinib improved iPFS over gefitinib in NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations and BMs (HR = 0.40, 95% CI: 0.23–0.71), regardless of the mutation type [22]. However, the PFS results were not presented. Numerous exploratory attempts have been made regarding the combination of EGFR‐TKIs with antiangiogenic therapy; however, conclusions remain inconsistent. For first‐generation TKIs combined with antiangiogenic treatment, patients with 21L858R mutation showed PFS benefits in trials like RELAY, NEJ026, ARTEMIS‐CTONG1509, and FL‐ALTER studies [23, 24, 25, 26]. However, the JO25567 and ACTIVE studies found no such benefits [7, 27]. In studies involving third‐generation TKIs combined with antiangiogenic therapy, RAMOSE study presented findings inconsistent with WJOG9717L study [28, 29]. Ramucirumab combined with osimertinib significantly prolonged PFS compared to osimertinib alone. However, the efficacy of this combination in patients with 21L858R mutation or BMs remains unclear. Additionally, in the context of EGFR‐TKI combined with chemotherapy, the GAP BRAIN study suggested that gefitinib combined with chemotherapy improved iPFS and PFS in patients with 21L858R mutation and BMs [16]. The FLAURA2 study explored third‐generation TKIs combined with chemotherapy, revealing that patients with 21L858R mutation or baseline BMs benefited from PFS [30]. These findings indicate that conclusions regarding various treatment modalities are inconsistent. Overall, current evidence for optimal treatment strategies for 21L858R mutation patients with BMs remains limited. Therefore, we conducted this retrospective study to explore optimal first‐line treatments for patients with 21L858R mutation and BMs, aiming to inform future clinical practices. Given the superior intracranial efficacy of third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs over first‐ and second‐generation TKIs, and that the efficacy data from first‐generation TKI combination therapies are comparable only to third‐generation TKI monotherapy, we first compared the efficacy of first‐generation, second‐generation, and third‐generation TKIs, both as monotherapy and in combination. The results indicated that third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs, whether used alone or in combination, exhibited superior efficacy in patients with EGFR 21L858R mutation NSCLC and BMs, underscoring the enhanced therapeutic effectiveness of third‐generation TKIs in managing BMs in NSCLC patients. Analysis of different treatment modalities within the third‐generation TKI cohort further elucidated the potential benefits of combination therapy. Notably, patients in Group B exhibited the longest median iPFS and PFS, highlighting the therapeutic advantage of combining third‐generation TKIs with chemotherapy. This finding aligns closely with the recent results from FLAURA2 study. Although the subgroup analysis of patients with baseline BMs in FLAURA2 study did not report iPFS and PFS data for those with 21L858R mutation.
Our findings suggest that for NSCLC patients with 21L858R mutation and BMs, treatment regimens containing third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs significantly outperform those with first‐ and second‐generation TKIs. This may be attributed to the superior intracranial efficacy of third‐generation TKIs, as first‐generation EGFR‐TKIs achieve only 1%–6% of their concentration in cerebrospinal fluid compared to peripheral blood [31, 32]. In contrast, animal studies show that osimertinib achieves significant brain exposure [33]. Current clinical research on first‐generation TKIs combined with treatment for BMs indicates that while combining first‐generation TKIs with chemotherapy or antiangiogenic agents improves efficacy, including in the 21L858R mutation subgroup, results remain inferior to those of third‐generation TKIs, as seen in the FLAURA, AENEAS, and FURLONG studies [8, 16, 17, 34, 35]. Therefore, for patients with BMs, first‐line treatment with third‐generation TKIs is preferred, including for those with 21L858R mutation. Our study suggests that for patients with BMs harboring 21L858R mutation, combining third‐generation TKIs with chemotherapy offers the best efficacy, with iPFS and OS not yet reached. Notably, direct comparisons demonstrated that this regimen achieved significantly longer iPFS, PFS, and OS than first‐generation TKI‐based combination therapies, underscoring its superior clinical benefit. Moreover, when compared with third‐generation TKI monotherapy and antiangiogenic combinations, the chemotherapy combination yielded improved survival outcomes, although the differences in PFS and OS between Groups B and C did not reach statistical significance. Regarding third‐generation TKIs combined with antiangiogenic therapy, Fang Wei et al. [36] reported that osimertinib combined with bevacizumab shows an iPFS of 26.7 months for NSCLC patients with BMs and 21L858R mutation. However, this study recruited only 28 participants. In the FLAURA2 study, the iPFS for the BMs subgroup treated with osimertinib in combination with chemotherapy has not been reached, with a reported PFS of 24.9 months [37]. The 21L858R mutation subgroup also showed a PFS of 24.7 months, suggesting that these patients are favorable candidates for this combination therapy. Regarding OS, analyses from the GAP BRAIN study, pooled data from BM subgroups of LUX‐Lung 3 and LUX‐Lung 6 studies, and the FLAURA study demonstrated no improvement for patients with 21L858R mutation [8, 16, 19], highlighting the challenge of enhancing survival for those with 21L858R mutation and BMs. The OS data from the FLAURA2 study remain immature; however, recent reports suggest that the combination therapy demonstrated an OS benefit trend in both the BMs subgroup and the 21L858R mutation subgroup [38]. Our study suggests that treatment regimens incorporating third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs significantly improve OS compared to those using first‐ and second‐generation TKIs. Additionally, the combination of third‐generation TKIs and chemotherapy showed a trend toward prolonged OS. However, the limited sample sizes in Groups B and C necessitate cautious interpretation of the results and restrict their generalizability. Nonetheless, the promising efficacy of this treatment approach in patients with 21L858R mutation and BMs from NSCLC warrants further validation in prospective randomized clinical trials.
Previous literature indicated that EGFR‐mutant NSCLC patients with concurrent mutations, particularly TP53 mutations, often had poorer responses to EGFR‐TKIs monotherapy [39, 40, 41, 42]. In some studies, the L858R mutation seemed more affected by TP53 co‐mutation compared to the 19del mutation [43, 44, 45]. While there are no specific treatment strategies for patients with concurrent mutations, combination therapies involving EGFR‐TKIs may be more effective. Retrospective and prospective studies indicated that combining EGFR‐TKIs with chemotherapy may provide greater benefits for patients with concurrent mutations [16, 46, 47]. Our analysis indicates that patients with concurrent TP53 mutations derive greater benefits from third‐generation EGFR‐TKI treatment compared to those receiving first‐ and second‐generation TKIs. These findings suggest that different concurrent genetic mutations may influence treatment decisions, highlighting the importance of a comprehensive evaluation of genomic profiles when formulating treatment strategies.
Regarding resistance mechanisms, consistent with previous studies, our data indicate that the emergence of the T790M mutation remains the primary mechanism of resistance in patients treated with first‐ and second‐generation EGFR‐TKIs, regardless of treatment type [48]. In contrast, the resistance mechanisms associated with third‐generation TKIs are more diverse. Our findings indicate that the primary resistance mechanisms to third‐generation TKIs include EGFR amplification, MET amplification, and TP53 mutations, which are consistent with existing literature [49]. The diversification of resistance mechanisms to third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs may stem from their broader target inhibition capabilities and the evolutionary pressures exerted by tumors. The third‐generation TKIs employ irreversible binding and inhibit T790M, prompting tumor cells to activate alternative escape pathways: bypass signaling compensation (e.g., MET amplification); EGFR‐dependent adaptation (such as EGFR amplification or novel mutations like C797S). Besides, our study highlights differences in resistance mechanisms between combination therapy and monotherapy with first‐ and third‐generation TKIs. Consistent with findings from ARTEMIS‐CTONG1509, FL‐ALTER, and previous retrospective studies, our data reveal a reduced incidence of the T790M mutation in patients receiving combination therapy with first‐generation TKIs [25, 26, 50, 51]. In patients receiving third‐generation TKIs combined with antiangiogenic therapy, the incidence of MET amplification has increased. Therefore, dynamic genomic testing to elucidate the resistance mechanisms associated with different treatment modalities is crucial for guiding sequential therapy and improving patient survival rates.
Although the combination of third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs and chemotherapy showed promising efficacy, its toxicity profile warrants attention. While no new safety signals were observed and the rate of treatment discontinuation was low, the incidence of grade ≥ 3 hematologic toxicities was relatively higher in this group, highlighting the need for careful patient selection and AE monitoring in clinical practice.
This study has several limitations. First, as a retrospective analysis, some data may be missing, and reporting bias is inevitable. The number of patients in Groups B and C was relatively small, necessitating cautious interpretation of the results. Additionally, the imbalanced sample sizes across treatment cohorts may have introduced selection bias and affected the interpretability of cross‐generation comparisons. Second, the diversity of EGFR‐TKIs and antiangiogenic agents used among the patient groups introduces significant confounding factors that may impact efficacy outcomes. Third, this study was based on data from one cancer center in China, which may not represent the real‐world experiences of hospitals at other levels. Fourth, first‐line combination therapy with third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs can significantly prolong survival in patients with BMs from NSCLC harboring the 21L858R mutation. Therefore, most patients in Group B have not yet reached the endpoints of intracranial progression and death, resulting in relatively immature data for iPFS and OS. Finally, due to the retrospective design, radiologic responses were not centrally reviewed by radiologists but were determined by investigators based on imaging reports and clinical records. This may introduce some degree of bias in response assessment.
Despite these limitations, this study provides preliminary clinical evidence supporting the combination of chemotherapy with third‐generation EGFR‐TKIs as the optimal first‐line treatment for patients with BMs from NSCLC harboring the EGFR 21L858R mutation, warranting further exploration.
